evidence: Voted against advancing S.3385, a three-year federal extension of enhanced ACA subsidies (Dec 2025); a federal extension, not state backfill.
Voted against the federal ROAD to Housing Act, which limits big investors' single-family purchases, citing federal control of housing (June 2026); federal bill, not state law.
Rated likely no on raising the federal minimum wage, saying government shouldn't guarantee a livable income (Oct 2020 Senate race survey).
Touted her AZRx state drug discount card, run through the multistate ArrayRx pool, saving $249 per prescription (Oct 2026); a discount card, not a price-setting board.
Budget proposal kept $44.8M to preserve the 40% high-quality rate boost in state child care aid (Jan 2026); targeted subsidy funding, not a universal system.
Lists one-time family tax rebates of up to $750 for 750,000 working families among her accomplishments (2023 budget); a one-time rebate, not a lasting credit.
Launched infrastructure districts, created by HB 2999 she signed in June, letting bonds finance roads and pipes to revive stalled housing (Sept 2026); law, not executive order.
Touted her consumer utility office winning $321M in savings by challenging rate hikes at the Corporation Commission (July 2026); no fee caps or lobbying limits.
Budget proposal adds $20M for early childhood education, including expanded access to early learning (Nov 2026); no universal pre-K pledge.
State of the State touted making Arkansas one of two states giving teachers 12 weeks paid maternity leave (Apr 2026); public workers only, not a state insurance program.
Touted her Arkansas Forward review finding $300M+ in savings by cutting waste and renegotiating contracts (Apr 2026); efficiency drive, not fraud audits or an inspector general.
Celebrated Arkansas' most-pro-life-state ranking, citing abortion limits she signed such as Act 973 and Act 485 of 2025 (Oct 2026).
Platform pledges to raise teacher pay to attract top educators and to create a defined-benefit retirement system (2026).
Platform would pause new data centers until rules pass and make data centers cover their own electricity costs, with local approval required (2026).
Platform would ban excessive drug markups and require hospitals and drug makers to disclose prices (2026); no state price-setting board.
Platform would create a governor's housing task force modeled on Atlanta's and an expedited permitting system (2026); no executive order named.
Platform would tax 'dark homes' owned by nonresidents (2026); targets absentee owners, not limits on large investors.
Platform pledges to defend the right to choose and contraception access (2026); no specific plan to write abortion rights into law.
